book:web_4dd132c9.description: A didactic poem on hunting, attributed to Oppian of Corycus (or possibly Oppian of Apamea), written in the 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Oppian adopted the erroneous opinion about hyenas.

book:web_56bbf1fb.description: Lost treatise on ancient luxury by the Cyrenaic philosopher Aristippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus' treatise to note Socrates' attachment to Alcibiades.

book:web_b194f611.description: A lost work by the Cyrenaic philosopher Aristippus (c. 435–356 BCE) that discusses natural philosophers, including Pythagoras.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus's work 'Account of Natural Philosophers' for an etymology of Pythagoras's name.

book:web_9b089814.description: Lost work by Aristippus of Cyrene (or possibly his grandson), cited by Diogenes Laërtius, containing anecdotes about ancient luxury.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius recounts a story from Aristippus's work about Periander's mother.

book:web_b894432d.description: A lost work by Aristippus the Younger (or possibly Aristippus of Cyrene), referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The treatise discussed anecdotes about ancient philosophers and their luxurious or amorous affairs.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus' work 'On Ancient Luxury' as stating that Xenocrates loved Polemo.
Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus for an anecdote about Aristotle's relationship with Hermias' concubine.
Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus's treatise 'The Ancient Luxury' as the source for Theophrastus's attachment to Nicomachus.

book:505222.description: In the early 1500s five men and five women find themselves trapped by floods and compelled to take refuge in an abbey high in the Pyrenees. When told they must wait days for a bridge to be repaired, they are inspired - by recalling Boccaccio's Decameron - to pass the time in a cultured manner by each telling a story every day. The stories, however, soon degenerate into a verbal battle between the sexes, as the characters weave tales of corrupt friars, adulterous noblemen and deceitful wives. From the cynica...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references a specific tale in the 'Heptameron' by the Queen of Navarre, disagreeing with its portrayal of a chaste encounter as miraculous, while also offering a brief positive comment on the book itself.

book:web_5d2c6e45.description: A prophetic book in the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament, attributed to the prophet Isaiah, traditionally dated to the 8th century BCE.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo notes that Ambrose recommended the book of Isaiah, and that he initially found it difficult.

book:web_bc0ebfd0.description: A collection of biographies of famous men, including a biography of Titus Pomponius Atticus. The 'Life of Atticus' is one of the surviving sections of this work.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne concludes with a quote from Cornelius Nepos to assert that individual character, rather than external power, shapes one's fortune.

book:web_64dc5f2b.description: Biography of the Athenian general Alcibiades, part of Nepos's 'De Viris Illustribus'.
commentaries: Polybius references Cornelius Nepos's work 'Alcibiades' as a source.

book:15953862.description: Drawn from James B. Atkinson and David Sices' Montaigne: Selected Essays, this annotated translation of Etienne de La Boetie's political masterpiece offers an ideal opportunity to become acquainted with the thought of a brilliant though short-lived sixteenth-century French thinker known for "his mortal and sworn hatred for all vice," as his friend Michel de Montaigne put it, "but particularly for that sordid traffic concocted under the honorable title of justice." Atkinson's Introduction fleshes out a portr...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne borrows this discourse by Estienne de la Boetie to adorn his own work, praising it as finely written and full, though noting it was written in youth and falls short of what Boetie might have achieved later.
Michel de Montaigne suggests that a brief comment in Plutarch may have inspired La Boetie's book 'Voluntary Servitude'.

book:web_aa1e3fbc.description: A collection of pastoral poems falsely attributed to the Roman poet Gallus (Gaius Cornelius Gallus, c. 70–26 BCE) in the Renaissance. The actual author is unknown, but the poems circulated under this pseudonym in the 16th century and were included in early printed editions of Virgil's works.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes a passage from Pseudo-Gallus's 'Eclogues' to illustrate the oppressive nature of life under strict regimens, using it to argue against depriving oneself of accustomed pleasures.

book:527507.description: In The Book of the Courtier (1528), Baldesar Castiglione, a diplomat and Papal Nuncio to Rome, sets out to define the essential virtues for those at Court. In a lively series of imaginary conversations between the real-life courtiers to the Duke of Urbino, his speakers discuss qualities of noble behaviour - chiefly discretion, decorum, nonchalance and gracefulness - as well as wider questions such as the duties of a good government and the true nature of love. Castiglione's narrative power and psychological...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Castiglione's 'The Courtier' for its opinion on the social disgrace of riding a mule.
Northrop Frye references Castiglione as the source of the concept of the 'graceful courtier,' which contributes to the thematic meaning of 'grace' in Renaissance comedy.
Erich Auerbach cites Castiglione's book 'Il Cortegiano' as the most famous illustration of the later fusion of Platonism and the courtly ideal.

book:web_70eadd48.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations. The work argued against Epicurean theology.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero cites Posidonius's observation that Epicurus's professed belief in the Gods was insincere, motivated by fear of public opinion.

book:web_c992f3de.description: A lost multi-book treatise by the Greek Stoic philosopher Posidonius, discussing celestial bodies. It is referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers' (c. 230 CE).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the seventh book of his treatise On the Heavenly Bodies stating the sun is pure fire.

book:web_6cbca3d6.description: A lost work on meteorology by the Greek Stoic philosopher Posidonius, written in the 1st century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in Meteorological Elements defining the world.

book:web_eb9c29f3.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, defining poetic expression as metrical or rhythmical diction. Referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 CE).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius' definition of a poetical expression from his work on style.

book:web_764d7627.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius of Apamea, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Posidonius's second book on Natural Philosophy for the doctrine of active and passive principles.

book:web_c3493513.description: Lost treatise on ethics by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, cited by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius refers to Posidonius' first book on Ethics for a proof of the reality of virtue.

book:web_22a5a3c8.description: A work on natural philosophy by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius of Apamea, now lost, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the fifteenth book of his Discussions on Natural Philosophy stating the world is spherical.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the second book of his Discourses on Natural Philosophy regarding the vacuum.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the first book of his Discourses on Natural Philosophy affirming the world is one.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's work on natural philosophy to explain the nourishment of the sun, moon, and stars.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's work on natural philosophy to define snow.

book:web_f2b0d182.description: Lost work on natural philosophy by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the sixteenth book of his Disclosures on Natural Philosophy stating the sun is larger than the earth.

book:web_5e3eaba3.description: A treatise on the gods by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the thirteenth book of his treatise On Gods discussing mind penetrating the world.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in his treatise On Gods claiming the heaven as the dominant principle.

book:web_cda60d95.description: A now-lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, entitled 'Exhortations' (Protrepticus), referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that Posidonius' Exhortations agree that virtue may be taught.

book:web_7d84e5a8.description: A lost philosophical treatise on duties by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's statement that the wise man will pray.

book:web_4ad0e310.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, likely written in the 1st century BCE, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's Exhortatory Essays for the idea that one should not abandon philosophy due to differing opinions.

book:web_ed99a490.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher and polymath Posidonius, likely a treatise on astronomy or meteorology, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Posidonius's third book of Heavenly Phænomena for the denial of substantial reality to a superficies.

book:web_2835d2f9.description: A lost work on meteorology by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius of Apamea, cited by later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's Meteorology for an explanation of the rainbow.

book:web_d8b0c5b7.description: A treatise on divination by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, now lost but referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's works on natural philosophy and divination to support the existence of divination.

book:web_0eb1a743.description: A philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, now lost, discussing the concept of fate.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's work on Fate to support the doctrine of fate.

book:web_8d4037e9.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius discussing the criterion of truth.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's 'On Criteria' for his opinion on right reason as a criterion.

book:web_81c0e1ed.description: A medical treatise by Galen on the properties of foods, written in the 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Galen's work De Alimentorum Facultatibus for the etymology of a term.

book:15777533.description:
Ideale rappresentante dell'autunno del Rinascimento, la Gerusalemme liberatadivenne ben presto uno tra i libri piu letti e amati in tutta Europa.
Tasso seppe descrivere con il suo poema un mondo umano e narrativo chiaroscurale, ricco di una tensione mai completamente risolta tra etica e desiderio, tra doveri nei confronti di una giustizia superiore e umanissimi cedimenti alle debolezze. Nel contrasto allargato alle grandi forze del Cielo e dell'Inferno, la Liberatacomunica un profondo senso di crisi attrave...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges uses Tasso's epic poem as an example of a work from which allegorical meanings can be derived.
Jorge Luis Borges discusses Tasso's 'Gerusalemme liberate' as a notable epic poem, contrasting it with its less successful revision.
Jorge Luis Borges references Tasso's epic poem as the third and least successful variation of a motif originating in Homer.
Northrop Frye lists Jerusalem Delivered as an example of a national epic from the high mimetic period, unified by patriotic and religious ideas.
Leo Tolstoy mentions Jerusalem Delivered as a work that must be judged by the same criterion.

book:web_e6634e53.description: A revised version of Tasso's epic poem 'Gerusalemme Liberata' (Jerusalem Delivered), written to conform more strictly to Counter-Reformation religious orthodoxy and Aristotelian literary principles. It is generally considered artistically inferior to the original.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Tasso's 'Conquistata' as a revised version of his epic that failed to achieve literary significance.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions Tasso alongside Milton and Virgil as poets committed to their craft.

book:web_1d05e6e6.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher and poet Timon of Phlius, likely containing satirical or philosophical verses, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Images as a source for Timon's verse about Pyrrho.
Diogenes Laertius cites Timon's 'Images' to illustrate the Sceptic position on evident appearances.

book:web_46fa978d.description: Satirical poem by Timon of Phlius, lampooning various philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Timon's 'Silli' as praising Thales as an astronomer.
Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Silli to describe Socrates.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Timon's work 'Silli' as containing a critique of Pythagoras.
Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Silli as a source for Timon's verse about Pyrrho.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Timon as Diogenes Laertius of the Silli, a work of satirical poetry.

book:web_00005d7f.description: Ancient Greek satirical poems by Timon of Phlius, referenced in Plutarch's Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch mentions that Speusippus is described in Timon's work as good at a jest.

book:9076267.description:
Testo latino a fronte.
A military leader of legendary genius, Caesar was also a great writer, recording the events of his life with incomparable immediacy and power The Civil Waris a tense and gripping depiction of his struggle with Pompey over the leadership of Republican Rome - a conflict that spanned the entire Roman world, from Gaul and Spain to Asia and Africa. Where Caesar's own account leaves off in 48 BC, his lieutenants take up the history, describing the vital battles of Munda, Spain and Thapsus,....
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Caesar's 'De Bello Civili' to illustrate that the Roman practice of fighting with rapier and cloak was similar to a contemporary custom.

book:web_54695c27.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Gallic Wars, written as a series of commentaries. The work was composed during the war (c. 58–50 BCE) and circulated in Rome. The abbreviation 'de Bell. Gallic.' is a standard Latin reference to this classic historical and military text.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Caesar's commentary on the Gallic Wars as a primary historical source regarding the geography and limits of ancient Germany.
Edward Gibbon cites Caesar's 'De Bello Gallico' as a source for information about the Germans.
Edward Gibbon cites a specific book (VI) and chapter (23) of Caesar's 'de Bello Gallico' (The Gallic War) as a footnote reference for information on German warfare and territorial practices.

book:web_1a35453b.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Roman Civil War against Pompey and the Senate, covering events from 49-48 BCE. Written as a continuation of his Commentarii de Bello Gallico.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Caesar's own 'Commentaries' on the Civil War as a source for his actions in defense of tribunitian rights.

book:551328.description: In this volume are three works concerning the campaigns engaged in by the great Roman statesman Julius Caesar (10044 BCE), but not written by him. "The Alexandrian War, " which deals with troubles elsewhere also, may have been written by Aulus Hirtius (ca. 9043 BC, friend and military subordinate of Caesar), who is generally regarded as the author of the last book of Caesar's "Gallic War.""The African War" and "The Spanish War" are detailed accounts clearly by officers who had shared in the campaigns. All t...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Hirtius's work 'de Bello Alexandrino' for a description of Alexandria.
Caesar is cited for his description of an animal in the Hercynian Forest that Cuvier identifies as a reindeer.
Suetonius discusses Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars as exemplary works.
Suetonius references Caesar's own account of sending a scout to Britain.

book:399578.description:
Reprint of the 1957 edition.
Book I of Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War starts with an account of Gaul and goes on to cover Caesar's defeat of first the Helvetians and then the Germans under Ariovistus. The Introduction to this edition of the Latin text, first published in 1957, gives background information on the Rome of Caesar's time, on Caesar himself and on the composition and reliability of his commentaries, on Gaul, and on the Roman Army. Useful maps are provided, along with Notes on the text,....
commentaries: Polybius compares Polybius's description of the Gauls with that given by Caesar in his work.
Suetonius references Julius Caesar's work 'Bell. Gall.' (Commentaries on the Gallic War) as asserting the opposite of Pliny's claim about Druidism.

book:19511472.description: This is a new edition of The Complete Commentaries of Julius Caesar. Including The Commentaries on The War in Gaul and The Roman Civil War. Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman and a distinguished writer of Latin prose. He played a critical role in the gradual transformation of the Roman Republic into the Roman Empire. Caesar's conquest of Gaul, completed by 51 BC, extended Rome's territory to the English Channel and the Rhine. Caesar became the first Roman general to cross both when he built a b...
commentaries: Tacitus cites Ascham's praise of Caesar's Commentaries, agreeing with the positive assessment of Caesar's work.
The index refers to Caesar's Commentaries as a work, indicating sections where this book is discussed.

book:web_5c9a05ff.description: Lost poem written by Julius Caesar in his youth, referenced in Suetonius's 'The Twelve Caesars'.
commentaries: Suetonius lists Cicero's youthful poem Glaucus Pontius and notes it was still extant in Plutarch's time.

book:web_18ed0ac4.description: A lost work by the ancient Greek grammarian Apion, detailing Egyptian history and culture, referenced by Aulus Gellius.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Aulus Gellius relates a story from Apion's work, with Apion claiming to have witnessed the event.

book:web_c4ca58bb.description: A fictionalized biography of Aesop, written in the Hellenistic period, blending legend and folklore about the legendary fabulist. It survives in later Byzantine recensions and is not attributable to a single known author.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this Hellenic text to illustrate how physical ugliness was attributed to Aesop, contrasting his moral and intellectual value with his appearance.

book:21331.description: A timeless collection of 80 of Aesop's best-loved fables--punctuated by the age-old morals that have instructed countless generations. This volume highlights such fables as "The Goose Who Laid the Golden Eggs," "The Mouse and the Frog," and the one and only "The Tortoise and the Hare."
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson cites Aesop's Fables as an example of a book that is not the work of a single author but of collective tradition.
Arthur Schopenhauer references Aesop's fables as a book given to children for educational purposes, noting the children's rationalist rejection of it.

book:web_2e915c7f.description: A foundational Christian apologetic work by Lactantius, written in the early 4th century, which systematically defends Christianity against pagan beliefs and philosophies.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lactantius's work as an example of early Christian rejection of the spherical Earth, using biblical literalism to argue for a rectangular cosmos.
Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius as a source of evidence regarding the choice of Constantine by his dying father.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lactantius for details on the financial inquisition and use of torture under Galerius.
Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius as a partial and injudicious source for an anecdote about a private conversation between Diocletian and Galerius, questioning its truth and decency.
Edward Gibbon quotes Lactantius to describe the rapid and improbable promotion of Maximin from humble origins to the rank of Caesar.
Edward Gibbon acknowledges Lactantius as a source that even praises the diligence and fidelity of the emperor Severus.
Edward Gibbon attributes a report about Galerius's long-term imperial schemes to Lactantius, while casting strong doubt on its reliability.

book:web_c7a2cf45.description: A theological work by Lactantius, also known as 'Divine Institutes', written in the early 4th century AD. It is an apologetic work defending Christianity against pagan critics and explaining Christian doctrine.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius's 'Divine Institutes' as a source describing prophecies of future calamities with eloquence.

book:web_677badd9.description: A lost work by Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Syrian philosopher, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers' (c. 230 AD). The text presumably discussed the Stoic philosopher Zeno of Citium.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Apollonius the Syrian's essay on Zeno as the source for Antigonus's letter.

book:web_906da3fd.description: A lost work by the 1st-century CE philosopher and wonder-worker Apollonius of Tyana, known only through fragments and references in later authors, collecting accounts of marvels and strange phenomena.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Aristeas is also mentioned by Apollonius in his work 'Hist. Mirab.'.

book:web_ce36d4e5.description: A collection of neo-Latin love poems (kisses) by the Dutch poet Johannes Secundus, first published posthumously in 1539. The work was highly influential in Renaissance poetry and inspired many imitations.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites the Basia as a pleasant modern work, though he questions if it fits the title of 'book'.

book:web_f120e8a2.description: A collection of moralizing letters by Spanish bishop and chronicler Antonio de Guevara, commonly known in English as 'Golden Epistles' or 'Familiar Epistles'. The work was widely popular across Europe in the 16th century.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions obtaining information from Guevara's 'Letters' (referred to as 'Golden Epistles') but expresses a low personal opinion of the work.

book:19308263.description:
Ce recueil est parfaitement mis en page pour une lecture sur Kindle.
Les Regrets est un recueil de poemes de Joachim du Bellay, ecrit lors de sa residence a Rome de 1553 a 1557.
Le recueil comprend 191 sonnets, dont certains en alexandrins. La forme adoptee par Du Bellay est nouvelle bien que le recueil soit de facture petrarquiste. Le sujet n'est pas l'amour pour une femme, mais pour son pays natal.
commentaries: Walter Pater credits M. Sainte-Beuve with identifying a quality of intimate poetry in Du Bellay's works.
Walter Pater credits M. Sainte-Beuve with identifying a quality of intimate poetry in Du Bellay's works.

book:web_ea6a4d5d.description: A collection of sonnets by Joachim du Bellay, first published in 1549, praising a half-imaginary lady named Olive.
commentaries: Walter Pater identifies Du Bellay's 'Olive' as a prime example of the traits of the Pleiad poetry.

book:web_39f082fe.description: A seminal literary manifesto of the French Renaissance, advocating for the enrichment and defense of the French language against Latin and Italian influences.
commentaries: Walter Pater identifies du Bellay's treatise as the inaugural text of the literary revolution, praising its modern critical insights.

book:web_a9724a7d.description: An epitome or summary of the lost work 'Succession of Philosophers' by Sotion of Alexandria, compiled by Heraclides (likely Heraclides Lembus, a 2nd-century BC Greek philosopher and historian). The original Sotion work dates to around 200–170 BC, and Heraclides' abridgment was produced in the 2nd century BC, well before 230 AD.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides' work 'Abridgment of Sotion' as a source listing poems attributed to Pythagoras.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Heraclides's 'Abridgment of Sotion' as a source claiming Epicurus was raised in Samos.

book:web_97e10f6b.description: A lost work by Heraclides of Pontus, an ancient Greek philosopher and writer (c. 390–310 BCE), likely summarizing earlier philosophical or historical material.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides' Abridgment for a detail about an Olympic victory.

book:17818767.description: Aeschylus was the first of the three ancient Greek tragedians whose plays can still be read or performed, the others being Sophocles and Euripides. He is often described as the father of tragedy: our knowledge of the genre begins with his work and our understanding of earlier tragedies is largely based on inferences from his surviving plays. Only seven of his estimated seventy to ninety plays have survived into modern times. Fragments of some other plays have survived in quotes and more continue to be disco...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aeschylus’s Agamemnon as a prime example of ancient textual density, using it to illustrate how translation must reconstruct the emotional and stylistic rhythm of original works.

book:237794.description:
Essa peca e considerada unica entre as tragedias remanescentes do periodo por retratar um evento historico - a guerra entre os gregos e os persas - em vez de dramatizar uma epoca distante, de herois miticos. A peca gira em torno do desastre em que os invasores da Grecia viram suas forcas navais aniquiladas pelos gregos na Batalha de Salamina.
A acao se passa na capital persa onde um mensageiro leva a rainha a noticia do desastre. Depois de atribuir a derrota da Persia a independencia e bravura gregas assim....
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Aeschylus's play 'The Persians' as an example of a tragedy associated with a historical occasion of national rejoicing, to argue against tragedy producing real sorrow.
Plutarch quotes Aeschylus' tragedy 'The Persians' as authoritative evidence for the size of the Persian fleet.

book:475080.description: A shrine is stronger than a tower to save, A shield that none may cleave. Step swift thereto, And in your left hands hold with reverence The white-crowned wands of suppliance, the sign Beloved of Zeus, compassion's lord, and speak To those that question you, words meek and low And piteous, as beseems your stranger state,
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Aeschylus's play 'The Suppliants' as an example to illustrate the musical structure underlying early drama.

book:web_5c157f8b.description: Ancient Greek tragedy attributed to Aeschylus, depicting the punishment of Prometheus for stealing fire from the gods and giving it to humanity.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche cites Æschylus' Prometheus as a contrast to the passive hero, discussing its thematic content.

book:web_b4e96174.description: A lost tragedy by Aeschylus, likely produced around 470 BCE, concerning the myth of the Eleusinian war and the recovery of the bodies of the Seven against Thebes.
commentaries: Plutarch references Aeschylus' play 'Eleusinians' as a source that provides a different account of events.

book:web_85a71847.description: A lost work attributed to Marcus Junius Brutus, the assassin of Julius Caesar, mentioned by Plutarch in his Life of Brutus. The book is no longer extant, but its existence is recorded in ancient sources.
commentaries: Plutarch mentions that Brutus wrote a book called 'Memoirs of Brutus' which is still extant.

book:web_02f930ae.description: A collection of historical anecdotes and sayings in nine books, compiled during the reign of Tiberius (14–37 AD). Commonly known as 'Memorable Deeds and Sayings' or simply 'Valerius Maximus'.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus as a source for an anecdote about a death caused by a grape-stone, exemplifying death's trivial causes.
Michel de Montaigne cites Valerius Maximus for an extreme example of thirst during a siege in Crete.
Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus's 'Factorum ac Dictorum Memorabilium Libri IX' to argue that compelled actions credit the enforcer rather than the performer.
Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus to critique the decline of military discipline.

book:551629.description:
Valerius Maximus compiled his handbook of notable deeds and sayings during the reign of Tiberius (14-37 CE). The collection was very popular in the Renaissance and has recently attracted renewed scholarly attention. Yet to date there has been no modern English translation of "Memorable Doings and Sayings." This work is now added to the Loeb Classical Library, a freshly edited Latin text facing D. R. Shackleton Bailey's pleasing and authoritative translation.
Valerius arranges his instructive examples in sho...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Valerius Maximus for a historical fact about the family.

book:web_7788b9a5.description: Collection of Latin poems by Scottish humanist, scholar and poet George Buchanan, first published in 1584. The work includes various poetic forms and celebrates Scottish themes.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Buchanan's 'Sylvae' as a poetic celebration of Scottish independence.

book:web_a4c92ca4.description: A lost work by Theodorus the Atheist (also known as Theodorus of Cyrene), a philosopher of the Cyrenaic school, from which Epicurus is said to have drawn key ideas.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Theodorus's book 'On Gods' and notes that Epicurus derived many of his ideas from it.

book:web_3953b152.description: A concise history of Rome from its founding to the reign of Emperor Valens, written in Latin by the historian Eutropius in the 4th century AD. It was widely used as a school text in antiquity and the Middle Ages.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Eutropius's work to provide historical details about the character and policies of the emperor Constantius.

book:web_dbe4d2bf.description: A geographical and political description of Greece by the ancient Greek philosopher and geographer Dicaearchus of Messana (c. 350–285 BCE). The work survives only in fragments, notably compiled in 'Geographi Graeci Minores' edited by Karl Müller (1855) and earlier in 'Geographiae Veteris Scriptores Graeci Minores' edited by John Hudson (1698–1712).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Dicaearchus's work to support an observation about the modest simplicity of private houses in ancient Athens.

book:web_b6c71cf3.description: A historical study of Russian foreign policy and influence in the Balkan region, published by Oxford University Press.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists two books by B. H. Sumner as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites this book to reference Dulles's explanation of the CIA's role.
Hannah Arendt cites Allan W. Dulles's statement to support the claim about the influential position of intelligence services in the U.S. government.

book:web_35c0f407.description: A legal and administrative work by Hans Frank, a prominent Nazi jurist and Governor-General of occupied Poland, published in Munich in 1939.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Frank's book to illustrate the ideological presentation of the Nazi regime as based on loyalty rather than dictatorship.

book:web_86a28b6d.description: A historical study of the Pan-German League (Alldeutscher Verband), a German nationalist organization active from 1890 to 1918, published as part of the 'Historische Studien' monograph series.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Werner's book as a source of useful information on the Pan-German League.

commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists a book by Raimund Schnabel as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_51a1550a.description: A multi-volume ethnographic work on Jewish customs, history, and contemporary life by German Christian Hebraist Johann Jacob Schudt. The first volume was published in 1714, with subsequent volumes appearing through 1717.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Schudt's work as a source of information on Jewish matters.

book:web_9adcd673.description: Historical work by French Catholic priest and historian Édouard Lecanuet, examining the precursors to the 1905 French law on the Separation of the Churches and the State. Published posthumously in 1930.

book:web_8e101aef.description: A scholarly work documenting the complicity of German academics and universities in Nazi ideology and the Holocaust, based on captured German documents.

book:web_f71cda6c.description: A comprehensive history of France from the French Revolution through the Third Republic, written by the Scottish historian and political commentator Sir Denis William Brogan.

book:web_9ae1e4a6.description: A collection of essays by French nationalist writer and politician Maurice Barrès, exploring nationalist doctrines and political scenes in late 19th-century France.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Barrès's book as a source on nationalist doctrines.

commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Ludendorff's book as a source, likely on supranational powers during WWI.

book:web_e80081d3.description: Swedenborg's first scientific periodical, published in 1716.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson mentions Swedenborg's publication of his scientific work Daedalus Hyperboreus.

book:web_82bcbb6a.description: A scientific and philosophical work by Emanuel Swedenborg, combining anatomy and spiritual insight, first published in Latin in 1744.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson praises Swedenborg's 'Animal Kingdom' as a poetic and unifying work of anatomy.
Ralph Waldo Emerson notes Swedenborg's declaration in this work about preferring analysis over synthesis.

book:web_88aed8db.description: A philosophical and scientific work by Emanuel Swedenborg, originally published in 1734, exploring natural philosophy and the principles of the universe.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson refers to Swedenborg's work Principia, describing it as a picture of original integrity.

book:web_2b2e41b0.description: Second volume in Anatole France's four-volume series 'Histoire contemporaine' (1896-1901), a satirical chronicle of French provincial life and politics during the Third Republic.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges identifies 'Mannequin d’osier' as part of Anatole France's series 'Histoire contemporaine'.

book:2425582.description:
This is the testament of Paul Baumer, who enlists with his classmates in the German army of World War I. These young men become enthusiastic soldiers, but their world of duty, culture, and progress breaks into pieces under the first bombardment in the trenches.
Through years of vivid horror, Paul holds fast to a single vow: to fight against the hatred that meaninglessly pits young men of the same generation but different uniforms against one another... if only he can come out of the war alive
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Remarque's novel as a counterpoint to Kipling's work, specifically in the context of war literature.

book:web_e6a4b658.description: A historical occult novel by Gustav Meyrink, blending the story of English occultist John Dee with a contemporary narrative.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges reviews a specific book by Gustav Meyrink, 'Der Engel vom Westlichen Fenster', indicating a direct citation of the work.

book:web_ffb933b7.description: A critical historical analysis of Christianity by the Scottish freethinker, journalist, and historian John Mackinnon Robertson.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Robertson's book to support an observation about the Gnostics and their method of constructing divine hierarchies.

book:web_b251d036.description: A monumental 15-volume compilation of travel narratives and geographical accounts from around the world, edited and compiled by Prévost. It was published between 1746 and 1759 and became a standard reference work on global exploration during the Enlightenment.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references the 'Histoire Generale des Voyages' as a source through which Rousseau and Nietzsche understood barbarous, pastoral life, unlike Hudson's firsthand experience.

book:web_56ed31bc.description: Early scientific work speculating about the possibility of life on the moon and methods of space travel, written by John Wilkins, an English clergyman, natural philosopher, and founder of the Royal Society.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Wilkins's book as a historical example of speculation about lunar habitation and travel, linking it to the development of science fiction.

book:web_dd05dd64.description: A 17th-century work proposing a universal language and philosophical classification system, published by John Wilkins, a founder of the Royal Society.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Wilkins' book as his speculative work on creating a world language, noting its physical dimensions and year of publication.

book:13298131.description:
The Book of Wonder is the seventh book and fifth original short story collection of Irish fantasy writer Lord Dunsany, considered a major influence on the work of J. R. R. Tolkien, H. P. Lovecraft, Ursula LeGuin and others. It was first published in hardcover by William Heinemann in November, 1912, and has been reprinted a number of times since. A 1918 edition from the Modern Library was actually a combined edition with Time and the Gods.
The book collects fourteen fantasy short stories by the author.
Sourc...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this collection as a key example of Dunsany’s mythopoeic horror, highlighting its eerie, fairy-tale-like entities that evoke cosmic dread through subtle suggestion.

book:web_b4b2d307.description: A Spanish translation (titled 'Paginas de historia y autobiografia') of selected historical and autobiographical writings by Edward Gibbon, published by the University of Buenos Aires in 1961.
commentaries: The excerpt lists this as a prologue written by Borges, indicating his engagement with Gibbon's historical and autobiographical work.
Harold Bloom lists Gibbon's historical work as a canonical text of great aesthetic interest.
The footnote identifies Edward Gibbon and his major work 'Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire', and includes a quotation from Carlyle about Gibbon.

book:web_3650c011.description: A biography of John Wilkins (1614-1672), English clergyman, natural philosopher, and founder of the Royal Society.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions consulting this biographical work on John Wilkins while researching for his note.

book:899896.description: The stories of twenty of Shakespeare's most popular plays
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites 'Tales from Shakespeare' by Charles and Mary Lamb as a preposterous example of paraphrase, using it to illustrate how interpretation can distort the original form.

book:web_4f086ab4.description: A collection of extracts from Elizabethan and Jacobean plays, with critical notes by Charles Lamb.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge praises Lamb's 'Dramatic Specimens' for its selections and original critical notes.

book:380793.description: Hadleyburg prides itself on a reputation of incorruptible citizens until an offended stranger vows revenge, trapping the most sanctimonious by letters promising a fortune. Also 14 short works of fiction and "truth": his reporter debut, rescue of shipwrecked sailors, his first lie comments on white lies, petition to Queen Victoria on taxes, "Esquimau Maiden's Romance", a detective story, and others.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes Twain's book to support an argument against racism and the idea of a chosen people, using it as authoritative commentary.

book:141312.description: Mark Twain's brilliant 19th-century novel has long been recognized as one of the finest examples of American literature. It brings back the irrepressible and free-spirited Huck, first introduced in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, and puts him center stage. Rich in authentic dialect, folksy humor, and sharp social commentary, Twain's classic tale follows Huck and the runaway slave Jim on an exciting journey down the Mississippi.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Twain's 'Huckleberry Finn' as an example of a novel where the hero and circumstances reciprocally change each other, similar to 'The Purple Land'.
Northrop Frye uses Huckleberry Finn to discuss the theme of freeing a slave and the ironic recognition scene in comedy.

book:1118948.description: In this mischievous yarn by Mark Twain, a Yankee mechanic named Hank Morgan is knocked unconscious in a fight and awakens to find himself at Camelot in AD 528. Brought before the Knights of the Round Table, he is condemned to death, but saves himself by using his nineteenth-century scientific knowledge to pose as a powerful magician. After correctly predicting an eclipse, Hank is made minister to King Arthur, and goes on to counsel him on such matters as gunpowder, electricity, and industrial methods. But w...

book:98935.description: "This book is the record of a struggle between two temperaments, two consciences, and almost two epochs. It ended, as was inevitable, in disruption. Of the two being here described, one was born to fly backward, the other could not help being carried forward..." Thus begins this remarkable chronicle of the division between generations. Goose was born in 1849 into a deeply religious household; both parents were pious member of the Plymouth Brethren, a narrow sect. This book, Gosse's masterpiece, was anonymou...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges states he is relying on a summary from Edmund Gosse's book because he could not find the original 'Omphalos'.

book:web_a0a5f548.description: A study of the language and jargon used by Spanish criminals in the late 19th century, written by criminologist Rafael Salillas.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Rafael Salillas' book to provide a counterexample of obscure Spanish slang, challenging Dr. Castro's claims about Argentine linguistic corruption.

book:web_8a522b2d.description: A lost work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Zeno of Elea, discussing Pythagorean doctrines.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists 'one on the Doctrines of the Pythagoreans' among Zeno's works.

book:web_93a731cf.description: Lost work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Zeno of Elea, known for his paradoxes and dialectical arguments.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Zeno's own work, 'Conversations', to illustrate his style of writing.

book:web_8d439258.description: A lost philosophical work by Zeno of Elea, known only through references in later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's work to explain the mechanism of a solar eclipse.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's work to explain the cause of lightning.

book:web_8d7f2413.description: A prose work by John Donne defending the thesis that suicide is not necessarily a mortal sin. Written circa 1608 but published posthumously in 1644.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges discusses Donne's treatise on suicide, its history, and its arguments.

book:web_949e4ae5.description: A satirical and metaphysical poem by John Donne, also known as 'Metempsychosis', written in 1601 and first published posthumously in 1633.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites Donne's 'Progress of the Soul' as an example of excellent poetic language.

book:web_8e80bda5.description: A philosophical and mystical work by Léon Bloy interpreting Napoleon Bonaparte as a providential figure and a symbol within a divine historical plan.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Bloy's book 'L’Ame de Napoleon' to illustrate the idea of history and human existence as a cryptic, sacred text.
Jorge Luis Borges describes Bloy's book 'L’Âme de Napoléon' as an attempt to decipher Napoleon as a symbol and precursor to another hidden hero.

book:web_369be336.description: A novel by French Catholic writer Léon Bloy, first published in 1905. The title translates to 'The Unsellable' or 'The Unsalable' and reflects Bloy's characteristic themes of poverty, faith, and social criticism.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Bloy's work 'L’invendable' as a text where he found different versions of Bloy's conjecture.

book:web_afb04fc5.description: A diary by French writer Léon Bloy, covering the years 1892-1895, first published in 1898.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Bloy's work 'Le mendiant ingrat' as a source from which he rescued versions of Bloy's conjecture.

book:web_cd72cd93.description: A novel by French Catholic writer Léon Bloy, published in 1911. The title translates to 'The Old Man of the Mountain' and is one of Bloy's later works of fiction.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Bloy's work 'Le Vieux de la Montagne' as another source containing fragments of Bloy's ideas.

book:web_70fc62f0.description: A book by suffragette and activist E. Sylvia Pankhurst advocating for the constructed international language Delphos, which she helped develop as part of the international language movement.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Pankhurst's book as a source consulted in his research on John Wilkins.

book:web_2dab9891.description: A study on Buddhism by the German historian and philosopher C. F. Koeppen, published in 1857.
commentaries: William James follows Koeppen's account.

book:web_9a709219.description: A scholarly work by Jesuit missionary and sinologist Léon Wieger, presenting Chinese biographies of Buddha with translations and commentary.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Wieger's collection of Chinese Buddha biographies to illustrate another variation where apparitions are godly metamorphoses.

book:web_57c73833.description: Historical work by Argentine writer Leopoldo Lugones about the Jesuit missions in South America, particularly the Jesuit reductions in Paraguay and surrounding regions.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes Leopoldo Lugones' book 'El imperio jesuitico' to support the point about Quevedo's reputation as an anecdotist.

book:1114472.description: Las fuerzas extranas reune doce relatos y una teoria del cosmos que constituyen los cuentos fantasticos mas perfectos de la literatura castellana y aun de la literatura. Perfectos por la prosa excepcional que los narra, por los argumentos asombrosos que abordan y por los hallazgos narrativos que Leopoldo Lugones ensaya para dar verosimilitud a estas fantasias. La vasta sombra de Edgar Allan Poe planea sobre ellos. Tambien la invencion de Wells, Villiers de L'Isle Adam, Leonardo da Vinci, Goethe y Marcel Sch...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references this short story collection by Leopoldo Lugones, noting its publication year.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions a book of poetry by Leopolda Lugones, providing its title and publication year.

book:958034.description: "Lewis is the ideal persuader for the half-convinced, for the good man who would like to be a Christian but finds his intellect getting in the way". --Anthony Burgess. The New York Times Book Review
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites C.S. Lewis's book as a further reference on the topic of suffering.
Jorge Luis Borges references Lewis's book as additional reading on the topic of suffering, following the citation from Bernard Shaw.

book:web_d59ed61d.description: A collection of translations by Dante Gabriel Rossetti of early Italian poetry, including works by Dante Alighieri and his contemporaries, with the poem 'Al cor gentil rempaira sempre amore' by Guido Guinizelli appearing on page 291 in the 1874 edition published by Ellis and White in London.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites a translated poem from an anthology.

book:22845779.description: Born in London to highly cultured Italian parents, the poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a passionate translator of the poetry of Dante Alighieri and his contemporaries. The Langley Press selection includes love sonnets not included in Dante's Vita Nuova, and others by poets including Guido Cavalcanti, Guido Orlandi and Cecco Angliolieri.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites a translated poem from an anthology.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions Machen's autobiography, 'The London Adventure,' as presenting a hypothesis akin to Bloy's regarding the symbolic nature of the external world.

book:web_8dbdf714.description: A short story by Arthur Machen, first published in 1915, blending mystical themes with the horror genre; it explores the return of ancient spiritual forces, tied to the Holy Grail legend and the context of World War I.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this work as a transcendent example of mysticism emerging from horror, linking it to the Graal legend and the wartime context.

book:21039781.description:
Print Length: 40 pages
Lucian of Samosata (125-c.180) was a Greek satirist of Syrian or Assyrian extraction, and True History is perhaps his most well-known tale. In this tale, the protagonist visits the Moon, meets extraterrestrial creatures, and takes part in interplanetary warfare. This piece of fantastical fiction parodies many works such as Homer's Odyssey, and is certainly a contender for the title of earliest science fiction story.
Many people could be forgiven for thinking that concepts such as voya...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Lucian's 'True History' as an early example of a fictional lunar voyage containing marvelous descriptions.

book:web_8e2c2db2.description: A dialogue by Lucian of Samosata praising friendship, in which a Scythian named Toxaris recounts stories of Scythian heroes and their war against the Bosporan Kingdom.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Lucian's 'Toxaris' as a literary source for a historical conflict, while noting its potentially fictional character.

book:7029455.description: This classic work is a general introduction to Indian philosophy that covers the Vedic and Epic periods, including expositions on the hymns of the Rig Veda, the Upanisads, Jainism, Buddhism and the theism of the Bhagvadgita. Long acknowledged as a classic, this pioneering survey of Indian thought charts a fascinating course through an intricate history. From the Rig Veda to Ramanuja, Radhakrishnan traces the development of Indian philosophy as a single tradition of thought through the ages. The author showc...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Radhakrishnan's work to support a description of the Buddhist concept of momentary thought.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Radhakrishnan's book to present a Buddhist perspective on the brevity of life, referencing a specific volume and page.

book:web_94f4a8e3.description: A collection of supernatural stories and ghostly encounters compiled by Lord Halifax, published in 1936.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges reviews a specific book attributed to Lord Halifax, 'Ghost Book', indicating a direct citation of the work.

book:web_c144e47d.description: Ancient Greek compendium of myths and heroic legends, traditionally attributed to Apollodorus of Athens but likely compiled by an unknown author in the 1st or 2nd century CE. It is a primary source for classical mythology.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Apollodorus's Bibliotheke for a myth about Orpheus and the sirens.

book:1935834.description: La obra de Quevedo editada aqui ha gozado a lo largo de los siglos de popularidad y tambien de consideracion controvertida. Los estudiosos se han planteado diversas cuestiones sobre la datacion, la fijacion del texto, la adscripcion o no al genero picaresco, la organizacion estructural, el sentido y significados ultimos de esta incomparable obra de ingenio. Domingo Yndurain traza en la introduccion un extenso panorama de estos problemas y de las distintas soluciones e ilustra el texto con abundantes y sabia...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Quevedo's 'Buscón' as an example of a purely successive narrative, criticizing Hudson for deviating from this simplicity in 'The Purple Land'.

book:69797.description: Tras haberse ejercitado en el modelo estructural de la picaresca de El Buscon, el mensaje de Quevedo, cada vez mas angustiado, se encauza en el genero de las visiones, de ascendencia tanto clasica como cristianomedieval. Con una satira cruel, repasa el universo de los vicios y pone de manifiesto su pesimismo radical sin solucion aparente.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Quevedo's book 'Sueño de la muerte' as an early use of the metaphor comparing dreams to theater.

book:pg14328.description:
Boethius composed De Consolation Philosophiaein the sixth century A.D. while awaiting death by torture, condemned on a charge of plotting against Gothic rule, which he protested as manifestly unjust. Though a Christian, Boethius details the true end of life as the soul's knowledge of God, and consoles himself with the tenets of Greek philosophy, not with Christian precepts.
Written in a form called Meippean Satire that alternates between prose and verse, Boethius' work often consists of a story told by Ovid...
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references Boethius's poems favorably when compared to his contemporaries.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Boethius's 'De consolatione Philosophiae' as a work whose author would not share the modern disdain for allegory.
Jorge Luis Borges references Boethius's 'De Consolatione Philosophiae' as a source for the Wheel of Fortune metaphor, suggesting Layamon could have used it if he had contemplated cyclical conquest.

book:web_7fe4ff44.description: A periodical publication by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, later collected into a single volume, containing essays on philosophy, politics, and literature. The 'Essay on Method' appears in the 1818 edition.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references an essay by Coleridge from this work, while noting his interpretation may not be strictly correct.

book:web_436ef14a.description: A collection of Coleridge's critical writings edited by Thomas Middleton Raysor, published by Harvard University Press in 1936.
commentaries: Northrop Frye directs the reader to Coleridge's collected criticism, noting an expansion of Coleridge's idea to clarify a critical principle.

book:web_c8fd8cee.description: A critical work by Samuel Taylor Coleridge exploring Greek classic poetry, based on his lectures and published posthumously.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references Coleridge's translation of a Homeric passage from his Introduction.

book:pg6081.description: Originally conceived as a short preface to Sibylline Leaves, by the time Coleridge's Biographia Literaria was published in 1817 it had expanded into a two-volume apologia for the Romantic poet's "literary life and opinions." Coleridge here develops a theory of the poetic imagination, in which an artist's passion, will, memory, and perception intersect to engender her or his work. This unique edition is essential to understanding the influences and ideology of Romanticism.

book:web_89aa67de.description: An unfinished philosophical work by Coleridge, announced in Biographia Literaria (1817) but never completed or published as a separate book. The reference is to a projected treatise within this work.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references his own forthcoming work, Logosophia, where he plans to elaborate on the Dynamic Philosophy.

book:web_17ea1505.description: A collection of elegiac love poems by the Roman poet Propertius, written in the 1st century BCE.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges notes that Quevedo's line is a recreation or exaltation of a line from Propertius's 'Elegies'.

book:115775.description:
The most famous work of Japanese literature and the world's first novel--written a thousand years ago and one of the enduring classics of world literature.
Written centuries before the time of Shakespeare and even Chaucer, The Tale of Genjimarks the birth of the novel--and after more than a millennium, this seminal work continues to enchant readers throughout the world. Lady Murasaki Shikibu and her tale's hero, Prince Genji, have had an unmatched influence on Japanese culture. Prince Genji manifests what w...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges discusses the translation of Murasaki's work, praising its naturalness and psychological depth, and comparing it to European literature.

book:web_662a5722.description: Historical work by Argentine writer and historian José María Ramos Mejía, analyzing the era of Juan Manuel de Rosas. The book contains controversial claims about the Jewish-Portuguese origins of many Buenos Aires families.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Ramos Mejia's book as a source listing family names to support a claim about Jewish ancestry in Buenos Aires.

book:814393.description: Dionysius of Halicarnassus was born before 53 BCE and went to Italy before 29 BCE. He taught rhetoric in Rome while studying the Latin language, collecting material for a history of Rome, and writing. His "Roman Antiquities" began to appear in 7 BCE. Dionysius states that his objects in writing history were to please lovers of noble deeds and to repay the benefits he had enjoyed in Rome. But he wrote also to reconcile Greeks to Roman rule. Of the 20 books of "Roman Antiquities" (from the earliest times to 2...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites a specific volume and page from Dionysius Halicarnassus's work on Roman antiquities as a footnote reference.

book:698911.description: Las ensenanzas del TAO TE CHING o <>, atribuido a LAO TSE (ca. s. v a.C.), pertenecen al amplio acervo de las sabidurias orientales antiguas. La esplendida version del poeta, traductor y estudioso practicante del zen Stephen Mitchell que aqui se ofrece esta regida por la intencion de traducir, mas que las palabras de la obra fundacional del taoismo, su idea. La complementariedad de los opuestos, el equilibrio, la obtencion de la plenitud mediante el desapego, la entrega al Tao, o absoluto, mediante el aband...
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites a specific verse from Lao-tse's foundational Taoist text.

book:3075730.description: Journalist, novelist, poet, artist and art critic, essayist, theologian, propagandist, philosopher, and creator of the wily old Father Brown - G. K. Chesterton is one of the most beguiling authors of the early twentieth century. When asked to perform a lecture tour in 1921, Chesterton was in a slump of depression. He had recently lost his brother to the First World War and his wavering faith in the face of the horrors of the conflict only intensified his malaise. 'What I Saw in America' tells us as much abo...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Chesterton's book to contrast the modern use of glowing eagles in commercial propaganda with Dante's celestial Eagle.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Chesterton's book on G. F. Watts as an analysis of allegory and later summarizes Chesterton's defense of allegory from it.

book:174852.description: A prolific and popular writer, G. K. Chesterton (1874-1936) is best known as the creator of detective-priest Father Brown (even though Chesterton's mystery stories constitute only a small fraction of his writings). The eight adventures in this classic British mystery trace the activities of Horne Fisher, the man who knew too much, and his trusted friend Harold March. Although Horne's keen mind and powerful deductive gifts make him a natural sleuth, his inquiries have a way of developing moral complications....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists this book as an example of Chesterton's repeated use of a particular narrative formula.

book:1011947.description: Gabriel Gale is an eccentric poet. His madness is the madness of insight and he uses this gift to solve or prevent crimes committed by madmen. Chesterton ably illustrates his own premise that lunacy and sanity may just be a point of view!
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists this book as an example of Chesterton's repeated use of a particular narrative formula.

book:1011931.description:
'The Paradoxes of Mr. Pond' is G. K. Chesterton's final collection of detective stories, published after his death in 1936.
The main characters in the book are Mr. Pond, his friend Captain Peter Gahagan, a romantic and impulsive Irishman, and a well-known government official, Sir Hubert Wotton. Also mentioned in more than one chapter are Violet Varney, an actress, and her sister Joan, to whom Gahagan proposes after being suspected of having an affair with Lord Crome's wife in "Ring of Lovers". Joan, now mar...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists this book as an example of Chesterton's repeated use of a particular narrative formula.

book:9114156.description: G.K. Chesterton's 1908 masterpiece, The Man Who Was Thursday, is a metaphysical thriller, and a detective story filled with poetry and politics. Gabriel Syme is a poet and a police detective. Lucian Gregory is a poet and a bomb-throwing anarchist. Syme infiltrates a secret meeting of anarchists and becomes 'Thursday', one of the seven members of the Central Anarchist Council. He soon learns, however, that he is not the only one in disguise, and the nightmare begins...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes a specific, nightmarish passage from Chesterton's novel to illustrate his tendency toward the atrocious.
Jorge Luis Borges references Chesterton's book as an example of literary imagination concerning wicked or unnatural forms.

book:web_b33c2170.description: A narrative poem by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, first published in 1842, expressing the speaker's disillusionment with the present and hope for the future.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson compares a line from Tennyson's poem to a similar thought.

book:web_2c522191.description: A poem by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, first published in 1830 in 'Poems, Chiefly Lyrical'.
commentaries: The footnote states that the lines are quoted from Tennyson's poem _Dirge_ and notes that they are misquoted from memory.

book:web_d1923a03.description: Roman author of a geographical compendium known as Collectanea rerum memorabilium or Polyhistor.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Solinus as a source for the Matronalia.

book:web_6a8c7fc0.description: A critical survey of American literature from colonial times to the early 20th century, originally published as 'Expression in America' in 1932.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Ludwig Lewisohn's book as one of several critical works on Hawthorne.

book:web_39279196.description: A collection of mystery stories featuring the Old Man in the Corner, a detective character created by Baroness Orczy. This was the third and final volume of stories about this character, following 'The Case of Miss Elliott' (1905) and 'The Old Man in the Corner' (1909).
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Orczy's work as a recent example of the detective story that similarly avoids physical action.

book:web_26907f78.description: A philosophical work by Josiah Royce, originally delivered as the Gifford Lectures, exploring metaphysical and epistemological issues concerning the individual and the absolute.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Josiah Royce's philosophical work 'The World and the Individual' for its analogy of a map containing itself, illustrating recursive infinity.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Josiah Royce's philosophical work to present a view on the nature of time that aligns with the essay's argument.
Jorge Luis Borges quotes Royce's work to present a view on the nature of time that he finds compatible with his own argument.

book:web_16329df8.description: Autobiography of Spanish writer, poet, dramatist, doctor, mathematician, priest, and professor Diego de Torres Villarroel, commonly referred to as 'Vida e historia' or 'Vida de Torres Villarroel'.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites a passage from this book as a second testimonial illustrating the fundamental incongruence of the self, noting Villarroel's description of himself as a cacophony of all human emotions and actions.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Kepler's 'Somnium Astronomicum' as a work that anticipates science fiction through its detailed lunar descriptions and attempt at verisimilitude.

book:web_3aab4620.description: A seminal work by the French philosopher and historian of medieval philosophy, Étienne Gilson, tracing the development of philosophical thought during the Middle Ages.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Gilson's book as a source for further reading on the scholastic commonplace regarding the two books.

book:web_8bb5595d.description: A seminal work by Étienne Gilson introducing and explaining the philosophical system of Thomas Aquinas. The citation refers specifically to the 3rd edition published in Paris in 1927.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach quotes Gilson's book 'Le thomisme' to support a point about Thomist anthropology and the provisional nature of earthly existence.

book:web_09bb9e22.description: Novel by Julien Green, originally published in French in 1930. The title translates to 'The Wanderer on the Earth' or 'The Traveler on Earth.' It is a psychological and metaphysical story exploring themes of alienation and spiritual searching.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references 'Le Voyageur sur la terre' as an example of a novel with an admirable plot from the current era.
Jorge Luis Borges cites this novel by Julien Green, providing its publication year.

book:web_809a2557.description: Book of gauchesco poems by Hilario Ascasubi, subtitled 'The Gauchos of the Rio de la Plata Singing and Fighting against the Tyrannies of the Republics of Argentina and Uruguay.'
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Ascasubi's book of gauchesco poems and provides its full title.

book:4293527.description: From almost the moment of its publication in 1667, Paradise Lostwas considered a classic. It is difficult now to appreciate how audacious an undertaking the epic represents, and how astonishing its immediate and continued success was. Over the course of twelve books John Milton wrote an epic poem that would "justify the ways of God to men," a mission that required a complex drama, the source of which is both historical and deeply personal. While the struggle for ascendancy between God and Satan is played ou...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Milton's epic poem as an example of a blind writer dictating and revising a major work.
Frances A. Yates discusses Milton's transposition of cabalistic motifs from Spenser into the openly Hebraic themes of his epic.

Northrop Frye lists Paradise Lost as an example of an epic, using it to define the customary use of the term 'epic'.

Northrop Frye references Paradise Lost to illustrate a tragic counterpart of the comic refuser of festivity.
Northrop Frye quotes Adam from Paradise Lost to exemplify a tragedy of innocence where the character survives and adjusts to new experience.
Harold Bloom describes rereading this epic poem to experience its originality and strangeness anew.
Harold Bloom analyzes the character of Satan in Milton's epic, comparing his role and downfall to Shakespeare's Iago.

Harold Bloom contrasts Mephistopheles with the Satan character from Milton's epic poem.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites Milton's PARADISE LOST as a work where scriptural material is suggested rather than directly used as the fable.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge reports an anecdote about Klopstock's high regard for the translation of Milton's work.

Ralph Waldo Emerson quotes a line from Milton's 'Paradise Lost' in a footnote.
