commentaries: Joseph Campbell references Rumi's 'Mathnawi' to illustrate the concept of an internal, psychological holy war.

book:web_eada549d.description: A psychological study of children's dreams by Charles William Kimmins, published by George Allen & Unwin in 1937. Kimmins was a British educational psychologist and Chief Inspector of Schools for the London County Council.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell references Kimmins's book to provide a specific anecdotal example of a child's dream.

book:web_bf48f70d.description: A comprehensive work on Shakta philosophy and Tantric traditions by the British jurist and scholar Sir John Woodroffe (also known as Arthur Avalon).
commentaries: Joseph Campbell bases a descriptive passage on Woodroffe's book.

book:web_e9871dec.description: An anthropological study of the Murngin people (Yolngu) of northeastern Arnhem Land, Australia, based on fieldwork conducted in 1926-1929. It is considered a classic ethnography of Aboriginal Australian social organization, kinship, and ritual.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites this book as a source of information on a specific cultural practice or belief.

book:web_74f97db9.description: A collection of Hindu and Buddhist myths retold and interpreted, originally published in 1913. Sister Nivedita (Margaret Elizabeth Noble) was an Irish-born teacher and author who became a disciple of Swami Vivekananda. Ananda K. Coomaraswamy was a pioneering Ceylonese Tamil philosopher and historian of Indian art.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell states that a preceding passage was adapted from this work.

book:web_90aac221.description: An ethnographic study of the Euahlayi people, an Aboriginal Australian tribe, documenting their customs, beliefs, and social organization.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites this book to provide a detailed account of a specific ritual involving sacrifice and cannibalism.

book:11133639.description: La Historia de la nacion chichimeca fue terminada hacia 1640. Y este titulo se debe a Carlos de Siguenza y Gongora quien fue propietario del manuscrito. Lorenzo Boturini, otro propietario del original, lo llamo Historia general de la Nueva Espana. Hay evidencia de que la Historia de la nacion chichimeca formo parte de un texto mas amplio que se ha perdido, o acaso no fue terminado. El capitulo final relata el Sitio de Tenochtitlan, desde la version texcocana de la Conquista promulgada por el autor;en contra...
commentaries: Joseph Campbell provides a detailed citation of a historical work by Ixtlilxochitl, including its publication history.

book:web_b3bafcdb.description: A comprehensive early work on Māori culture, history, and the natural history of New Zealand by Reverend Richard Taylor, an English missionary and ethnographer.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites a specific book by Reverend Richard Taylor on New Zealand and its inhabitants.
James George Frazer cites this book as a source for New Zealand customs.

book:web_c75b50a1.description: A comprehensive work on Slavic mythology, published in Prague. An English abridgment was later published as 'Slavic Mythology' in 1918 as part of 'The Mythology of All Races' series.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites Máchal's book as the foundational source for Mansikka's discussion of Slavic mythological spirits.
Joseph Campbell cites a specific volume and pages from Toynbee's historical work.

book:web_00cbf1d7.description: A scholarly work on Indian mythology by the noted German Indologist Heinrich Zimmer, published in Stuttgart and Berlin in 1936.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell bases his discussion of Indian myths on Zimmer's book, using it as a source text.

book:web_217725b1.description: A translation and compilation of key texts from the Zohar, the foundational work of Kabbalah, by the occultist and co-founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell references a specific translation of a cabalistic text, citing the translator and the book's title.

book:web_0758fb9c.description: A detailed anthropological study of the Hako ceremony of the Pawnee people, published as part of the Twenty-second Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites Fletcher's ethnographic report on a Pawnee ceremony, including a direct quotation from a priest.

book:web_51e76620.description: Early 20th century ethnographic work on Māori culture and life in New Zealand (Ao-tea being an early name for New Zealand), published by Whitcombe and Tombs.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites a specific book by Johannes C. Anderson on Maori life.

book:162695.description: The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishnais published by The Ramakrishna-Vivekananda Center of New York which bases it teachings on the principles of Vedanta, or Hinduism. Hinduism teaches that every soul is potentially divine, and that its divinity may be manifested through worship, contemplation, unselfish work, and philosophical discrimination. According to Hinduism, Truth is universal and all humankind and all existence are one. It preaches the unity of the Godhead, or ultimate Reality, and accepts every faith as a...
commentaries: William James quotes Ramakrishna from the book 'his Life and Sayings'.

book:web_28ac3292.description: A foundational anthropological work documenting the customs, social organization, and rituals of the Arrernte (Aranda) and other Indigenous peoples of central Australia.
commentaries: Joseph Campbell cites Spencer and Gillen's ethnographic work for information on subincision practices among Australian tribes.

book:3746210.description: Written five centuries ago by a humble monk, this timeless message of faith in Christ's teachings remains a vital source of spiritual strength for people seeking to follow in the footsteps of the Lord.
commentaries: Matthew Arnold quotes Matthew Arnold of the Imitation of Christ on the difficulty of the path to perfection.
William James quotes the Imitation of Christ as an example of genuine Christian outpouring, contrasting it with the Stoic passage from Marcus Aurelius.
William James references this work in the index, likely as a source of religious inspiration.

book:web_52f833b9.description: Book by Joseph Butler, first published in 1736, arguing by analogy for the consistency of natural and revealed religion.
commentaries: Charles Darwin quotes Butler's Analogy of Revealed Religion as an epigraph.

book:43958.description: A highly influential figure in the Church of England, John Henry Newman stunned the Anglican community in 1843, when he left his position as vicar of St. Mary's, Oxford, to join the Roman Catholic church. Perhaps no one took greater offense than Protestant clergyman Charles Kingsley, whose scathing attacks against Newman's faith and honor inspired this brilliant response. Apologia Pro Vita Sua,Newman's spiritual autobiography, explores the depths and nature of Christianity with flowing prose and a conversat...
commentaries: Matthew Arnold references Dr. Newman's Apology as a source to understand the Oxford movement's opposition to liberalism.
William James quotes Newman's autobiographical reflections on dogma and his relationship with ecclesiastical authority.

book:web_d4949d0a.description: A series of theological lectures by John Henry Newman, first published in 1838, exploring the doctrine of justification in Christian theology.
commentaries: William James references Newman's work as containing a passage that illustrates an aesthetic approach to Christianity.

book:449250.description: The issues that John Henry Newman raised--the place of religion and moral values in the university setting, the competing claims of liberal and professional education, the character of the academic community, the cultural role of literature, the relation of religion and science--have provoked discussion from Newman's time to our own.
commentaries: William James cites Cardinal Newman's The Idea of a University as a work that expresses disdain for sentiment and insists on theology as a science.
Samuel Taylor Coleridge identifies George Herbert as an exquisite master of a particular style and then proceeds to quote from his work.

book:web_34b756e1.description: A comprehensive study of Roman mythology by the German classical philologist Ludwig Preller, first published in 1858.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Preller's Römische Mythologie (third edition) as a reference in the discussion of Veturius.
James George Frazer cites Preller, Roscher, and Usener together when describing the ceremony and the role of the Salii.

book:web_ad923757.description: A comprehensive work on Greek mythology, first published in 1854 and later revised. Ludwig Preller was a German classical philologist.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Preller's Greek Mythology as a source.

book:1629151.description:
The Second Epistle to the Corinthians [NICNT] illuminates the historical background of the church at Corinth and clarifies the meaning of Paul's passionate letter both for those first-century Christians and for today.
Barnett assumes and offers argument for the unity of the letter and takes the view that Paul is addressing the issue of triumphalism in Corinth expressed by the newly arrived missioners who portray Paul as inferior to themselves. It is also endemic among the Corinthians and according to Barnet...
commentaries: Matthew Arnold compares St. Paul's argumentation in the Epistle to the Corinthians with Plato's in the Phaedo, finding both inadequate.

book:web_08ee8278.description: A travelogue and study of Mormonism, published anonymously as 'by One of Themselves' but actually written by the English journalist and historian William Hepworth Dixon.
commentaries: Matthew Arnold references Hepworth Dixon's book on the Mormons to illustrate a point about how people uncritically accept doctrines based on the number of followers or rifles.

book:web_8af07ba9.description: A historical work by John Knox covering the Scottish Reformation.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle references Knox's History as a work that displays his drollery and true eye for the ridiculous.

book:web_a0ddf6e3.description: The central religious text of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the word of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Gabriel, compiled into a book after his death.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle describes the Koran as the work dictated by Mahomet, regarded by his followers as a miracle and the standard of all law and practice.
Ralph Waldo Emerson quotes a passage from the Koran as a 'trumpet-text' to contrast with Shakespeare's use of nature.

book:web_20762c71.description: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle attributes the divine Hebrew book to Moses, describing it as the word of Moses and crediting it with building St. Paul's Cathedral.

book:web_c883f662.description: A four-volume historical work by William Godwin, covering the English Commonwealth period, published between 1824 and 1828.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle references William Godwin's historical work on the Commonwealth to note that even a diligent historian cannot explain the Parliament's final answer.

book:web_a212c7fa.description: Samuel Turner's firsthand account of his diplomatic mission to Tibet in the late 18th century.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle references Turner's book as a source of insight into the beliefs of the Thibet people, suggesting it provides a truthful perspective on Grand Lamaism.

book:web_e76b3261.description: A lost philosophical work by Xenocrates of Chalcedon, discussing the doctrines of Speusippus and Xenocrates himself, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: The subject wrote a book on the philosophy of Speusippus and Xenocrates.

book:web_1c0a8877.description: Lost historical memoirs by Aratus of Sicyon, a Greek statesman and general (271–213 BCE), cited by Plutarch in his Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch references Aratus's own commentaries to contradict a local religious tale about the battle, citing Aratus's account of the military action instead.
Plutarch cites Aratus's commentaries where he denies involvement in the attempt on the Piraeus, blaming Erginus instead.

book:web_1822bd1f.description: A lost Roman comedy by Caecilius Statius, quoted by Cicero in Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero quotes Statius's play 'Synephebi' as an example of human concern for posterity, which he uses to argue for the immortality of the soul.
Marcus Tullius Cicero quotes a line from Statius's play Synephebi to dramatize his appeal to the public regarding religion.

book:web_6c6d6929.description: Lost historical work by Timaeus of Tauromenium, composed in the 3rd century BCE, covering the history of Sicily. Only fragments survive.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero cites Timaeus as a source for the description of Syracuse.

book:web_13a069ea.description: A lost work by the Peripatetic philosopher Dicæarchus of Messina, containing dialogues held at Mytilene arguing for the mortality of the soul.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions Dicæarchus's three books 'Lesbiacs' arguing for the mortality of the soul.

book:web_63423a85.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Diogenes of Seleucia (Diogenes the Babylonian), who wrote on the allegorical interpretation of Athena's birth from Zeus. The text is known only through references in later authors such as Cicero.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero cites Diogenes the Babylonian's book 'A Treatise concerning Minerva', noting its content regarding the birth of Minerva.

book:web_6132e160.description: Lost work by the Stoic philosopher Diogenes of Seleucia (Diogenes the Babylonian), discussing the nature of voice and hearing.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diogenes of Babylon's 'On the Voice' for the definition of voice.

book:web_61d26702.description: An epic poem by the Roman poet Gnaeus Naevius, composed around 235 BCE, recounting the First Punic War. It is one of the earliest works of Latin literature.
commentaries: Suetonius references Naevius's work 'Punic War'.

book:web_c881bbff.description: Lost work by Aristoxenus, a Peripatetic philosopher and music theorist, containing historical anecdotes about philosophers, including the story that Plato wished to burn all writings of Democritus.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristoxenus's work for the story that Plato wanted to burn Democritus's writings.

book:web_0eac6096.description: A biography of Plato written by the Peripatetic philosopher and music theorist Aristoxenus. The work is now lost but was cited by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Aristoxenus's work 'Life of Plato' is the source for the seventh Aristotle.

book:web_7aefe6df.description: Lost work by Aristoxenus, a 4th-century BC Greek philosopher and music theorist, detailing the life and circle of Pythagoras.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristoxenus' work for an account of Pherecydes' death and burial.

book:web_c9b38daf.description: A treatise on diseases by the Greek philosopher Heraclides of Pontus, referenced by Diogenes Laertius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides' medical treatise as a source for Empedocles' communication with Pausanias.

book:web_e189c24f.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher Alcidamas, mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius. It discusses natural philosophy and claims Zeno and Empedocles were pupils of Parmenides.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Alcidamas's work 'Natural Philosophy' as a source for the philosophical lineage of Zeno and Empedocles.
Augustine describes reading the Psalms and being kindled towards God.

book:web_cf84c8b9.description: A historical treatise on English boroughs and their charters, written by the antiquary and historian Thomas Madox.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Madox's work as a source for information about adulterine guilds and fines paid to the king.
Adam Smith cites Madox's works to support the practice of farming town revenues to burghers.
Adam Smith again references Madox's work, along with Pfeffel, regarding jurisdictions granted to towns.

book:web_7918be44.description: A multi-volume history of New France (French colonies in North America) written by Jesuit historian Charlevoix, first published in 1744.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Charlevoix's history.
James George Frazer cites Charlevoix's history of New France.

book:web_d6b27036.description: A collection of tracts on the corn trade and corn laws, written by Charles Smith and referenced by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites the quantitative estimate of the average corn import from this work.

Adam Smith cites Adam Smith of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade as an authority on the effects of the corn bounty, noting his argument that the value of exported corn exceeds that of imported corn plus bounties.

book:web_5ba05e33.description: A historical and legal treatise on English poor laws, written by the English legal writer and clergyman Richard Burn.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Doctor Burn's work 'History of the Poor Laws' to discuss the hardship of certificate requirements.

book:web_4b5fefdb.description: A pamphlet proposing a scheme for poor relief by Sir Matthew Hale, likely published posthumously.
commentaries: Smith references Hales's computation of a labourer's family expenses and notes that Hales researched the subject carefully.

book:web_aa7a1c40.description: A work on the wool trade by the Reverend John Smith, referenced by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites John Smith's work to support the claim that English wool prices are depressed below those of inferior wool in Amsterdam.

book:web_97977356.description: A historical account of Massachusetts Bay Colony by Colonial Governor Thomas Hutchinson, originally published in multiple volumes. Volume 2 was published in 1767.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Hutchinson's History of Massachusetts Bay as a source for the fact that the colony paid off most of its public debts with a tenth of the original value of its paper money.

book:web_186dc1cb.description: A critical examination of Du Tot's economic treatise, published in 1740.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Mr Du Verney's book as a clear explanation of the Mississippi scheme's operations.

book:web_42706606.description: A work by the French physiocrat Pierre-Paul Mercier de la Rivière, originally published in 1767 as 'L'Ordre naturel et essentiel des sociétés politiques.'
commentaries: Adam Smith cites this book as the clearest exposition of the Economists' doctrine.

book:web_c95a675b.description: A foundational work of mercantilist economic theory, published posthumously in 1664, arguing that a nation's wealth is measured by its stock of precious metals and advocating for a positive balance of trade.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Mun's book as a work whose title became a fundamental maxim in political economy.

book:web_db6cbe64.description: A book on commerce by Mr. Meggens, with a postscript added in 1756 correcting errors.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Mr Meggens' book 'Universal Merchant' and its postscript as a source for data on the annual importation of precious metals into Spain and Portugal.

book:web_eb9236d3.description: Historical work covering the Holy Roman Empire, including events under Frederick II and the Hohenstaufen dynasty.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Pfeffel's work on remarkable events under Frederick II and his successors.

book:web_ac85aa5d.description: Travelogue by Pierre Poivre recounting his journeys and observations in Asia, particularly Cochin China and other regions.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Mr Poivre's observations on the price of sugar in Cochin China.
Adam Smith cites Kalm's observations on North American colonial husbandry as evidence for a system of agriculture similar to that in Scotland.

book:web_4ea684a8.description: A monumental medieval Latin glossary, often referred to as Du Cange's Glossary, first published in 1678, with later editions including the Benedictine edition.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Du Cange's glossary as a source for the account of King John of France's coin adulteration.

book:web_782d3107.description: A treatise on economics proposing the use of paper money backed by land, written by Scottish economist John Law.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Mr Law's own discourse as explaining the principles of his project.

book:web_565ee344.description: A comprehensive historical account of commerce by the Scottish economist and agriculturalist James Anderson, first published in 1764.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Anderson's work to support a critical assessment of the Hudson's Bay Company's profits, noting that Anderson's analysis of Dobbs' accounts shows the profits were not extraordinary.

book:web_88fc1f85.description: An early economic treatise on grain policy, addressing regulation and trade of grain in France.
commentaries: Adam Smith references the 'elegant author' of the 'Essay on the Policy of Grain' as an observer of the decline in grain prices in France.

book:web_48bd4b9e.description: A historical work by Robert Brady (c. 1627–1700), an English historian and physician, originally published in 1690. It discusses the history and legal status of English cities and boroughs.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Brady's work as a source for imperfect accounts from Doomsday-book regarding taxes paid by burghers.

book:web_6c9a8a92.description: A historical account of British public revenue, referenced by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites this work as a source for the figures on public debt accumulation.

book:web_f71b9442.description: A philosophical and historical work by Scottish philosopher and judge Henry Home, Lord Kames.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Lord Kames' work as a source for a point about smuggling penalties.

book:web_c228a0a6.description: A seminal work by Jesuit missionary José de Acosta, first published in Spanish in 1590, covering the natural history, geography, and indigenous cultures of the New World.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Acosta's work as a source describing a Mexican festival.

book:web_8819d01a.description: A natural and moral history of the Indies, originally published in Spanish as 'Historia natural y moral de las Indias'.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Acosta's history as a source for Mexican sacrificial customs.

book:web_42fadc19.description: A work by Bernardino Telesio (Bernardinus Telesius) that critiques Aristotelian natural philosophy and proposes a new system based on principles derived from nature itself.
commentaries: The editor notes that Telesius wrote a work combating the Aristotelian system, titled 'De Rerum Natura juxta propria principia'.

book:web_2fab096d.description: Foundational multi-volume work on human physiology by Swiss anatomist and physiologist Albrecht von Haller, published between 1757 and 1766.
commentaries: The editor cites Haller's work in physiology as having thoroughly covered the subject.

book:web_22084a9c.description: A philosophical work by Franciscus Patricius (Francesco Patrizi), published in 1593, opposing Aristotelianism and proposing a new system of natural philosophy.
commentaries: The editor mentions Patricius's work 'Nova de Universis Philosophia' as an attack on Aristotle and a proposal for a new philosophy.

book:web_d5aa9e95.description: Foundational work on magnetism and electricity, published in 1600.
commentaries: The editor praises Gilbert's work as a complete and enduring foundation of the science of magnetism.
Boethius references Tylor's book in a footnote to explain a superstition about the moon.

book:web_37f1eae0.description: A work on Stoic philosophy by the German historian of philosophy Eduard Zeller, originally part of his larger history of Greek philosophy and translated into English.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references Zeller's book on the Stoics for further information.

book:web_7a8fb912.description: A historical work by Pompeius Trogus covering the Macedonian empire and world history, surviving mainly through an epitome by Justin.

book:web_dc0ef02b.description: A comprehensive botanical manual by Asa Gray, first published in 1848 and updated in multiple editions, covering the flora of the northern United States.

book:web_204cccdf.description: One of the Bridgewater Treatises, discussing geology and paleontology in relation to natural theology.
commentaries: Charles Darwin cites Buckland's observation that fossils fill gaps between living groups.

book:web_1b16a704.description: British naturalist and curator; his account of Bermuda's natural history was referenced by Charles Darwin in On the Origin of Species.
commentaries: Charles Darwin cites Mr. J. M. Jones's account of bird migrations to Bermuda.

book:web_71fa5894.description: A comprehensive physical atlas containing data on ocean currents, among other geographical features, referenced by Darwin in 'On the Origin of Species'.

book:web_7c4009e5.description: Account of Gmelin's travels through Siberia as part of the Great Northern Expedition, originally published in multiple volumes.

James George Frazer cites Gmelin's travel through Siberia.

book:web_5d44109f.description: A scientific work by Richard Owen, published in 1849, discussing the comparative anatomy and homology of vertebrate limbs, referenced by Darwin in 'On the Origin of Species'.
commentaries: Charles Darwin cites Owen's work on limbs to support the argument about the difficulty of explaining homology by utility or final causes.

book:web_363557ca.description: A collection of essays by the German philosopher Christian Garve, first published in 1779.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge lists this as a work by Christian Garve.

Paine wrote: "Of all the tyrannies that affect mankind, tyranny in religion is the worst; every other species of tyranny is limited to the world we live in; but this attempts to stride beyond the grave, and seeks to pursue us into eternity."
The cool rationale of Paine's The Age of Reasoninfluenced religious thinking throughout the world; and its pervasieve influence continues to the...
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge associates Thomas Paine's work with declamatory and ranting religious discourse, criticizing it as rude.

book:web_5fe1aa55.description: A book examining natural and artificial systems of philosophy, published in 1812 by Richard Saumarez.

book:web_98035b31.description: British surgeon and physiologist, author of 'A New System of Physiology' (1797) and other works on philosophy and science.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge praises Saumarez's works, especially his first, and notes his original views on dynamic philosophy.

book:web_a10c38cc.description: A botanical treatise by the Italian scholar Julius Caesar Scaliger, often cited in early modern discussions of natural philosophy and ethics.

book:web_c352f683.description: A burlesque translation of Virgil's Aeneid by Charles Cotton, originally published as 'Scarronides, or, Virgile Travestie'.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references Cotton's Poems and his Virgil Travestied as containing specimens of excellent poetic style.

book:web_2060cd32.description: A collection of religious meditations by James Hervey, often referred to as 'Hervey's Meditations', first published in the mid-18th century.

book:web_2b758556.description: Epic poem in hexameters on the life of Christ, originally published in the first four cantos in 1748, with later expansions completed in 1773.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge mentions that he has read the first four books of Klopstock's epic poem and is asked for his opinion.

book:12976649.description: (Lovecraftian horror short story) "I always assumed that my extreme ugliness was the principal reason why I was kept secluded from the world. I accepted the logic of this without question, never suspecting that perhaps darker matters concerning familial degeneracy and certain violations of natural law might have played a greater par...
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge refers to Wordsworth's poem 'The Recluse' as an example where Wordsworth speaks in his own person even through different characters.

book:web_b4cae0dd.description: A Spanish auto sacramental play from the 16th century, also known as 'Atheista Fulminato'. It is referenced by Samuel Taylor Coleridge in his 'Biographia Literaria' as an old Spanish play performed in churches and monasteries.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references this old Spanish play as a comparison to the German drama, noting its imaginative nature and popularity across Europe.

book:web_6bff7b4b.description: A collection of academic orations and literary critiques by the Jesuit writer Famiano Strada.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites Strada's Prolusions as a source for poetic diction.

book:web_3053a7ad.description: A collection of verse epistles by the Elizabethan poet Samuel Daniel, first published in 1603 as part of his 'Certaine Small Workes'.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge mentions Daniel's 'Epistles' and 'Hymen's Triumph' as containing fine examples of a style midway between prose and verse.

book:web_c111623f.description: A pastoral tragicomedy by Samuel Daniel, first published in 1615.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge mentions Daniel's 'Hymen's Triumph' alongside his 'Epistles' as containing fine examples of a style midway between prose and verse.

book:web_159c1dcd.description: An epic poem by Samuel Daniel, first published in 1595, chronicling the Wars of the Roses between the Houses of Lancaster and York.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references Daniel's 'The Civil Wars' as an instructive work, and uses stanzas from it to illustrate prosaic style.

book:31427876.description:
Originally written in German, Oberon is a very long form heroic poem. Huon of Bordeux, a mighty but flawed French crusader with Charlemagne, has many adventures in the Middle East and during his difficult journey home.
Oberon duels. He is attacked and kills his attacker, leading to a curse. Oberon meets a Muslim woman. They fall in love, and she converts. They are hunted, imprisoned, escape, and nearly starve on a magical island in the Mediterranean.
After several amazing adventures and having overcome the....
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge describes a conversation about Wieland's epic poem, which he found flawed.

book:235390.description: George Fox's record of his life and ministry is a Christian classic. Its pages chroncile not only Fox's spiritual travial when he heard a voice that said, "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition," but his years of ministry and gathering a people for Christ who became known as the Society of Friends. Includes a glossary of words and phrases most commonly used by Fox.
commentaries: William James quotes George Fox's Journal to describe the early Quakers' battle for social veracity and sincerity.
William James quotes from George Fox's Journal to illustrate the isolation of first-hand religious experience.

book:web_2027ed87.description: A work on English synonyms by William Taylor, referenced by Coleridge in Biographia Literaria.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge mentions Mr. W. Taylor's recent volume of synonymes but notes he has not seen it, and defers to Wordsworth's criticism of it.

book:web_196645b1.description: A popular 18th-century medical guide for domestic use.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references Dr. Buchan's domestic medicine book as providing advice similar to requests for unbiased reading, which he finds unrealistic.

book:web_351fb6fa.description: A historical work covering Scotland from the Union of the Crowns (1603) to the Union of the Kingdoms (1707), authored by Malcolm Laing, a Scottish historian.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites Laing's historical work as a reference.

book:web_87c8313b.description: A topographical poem by William Crowe, first published in 1788, describing the hill Lewesdon in Dorset, England.

James George Frazer cites Mannhardt's work on folklore.

James George Frazer cites Riedel’s work on the races of the region.

commentaries: James George Frazer cites this travel book for West African customs.

book:981024.description:
Joel Brouwer writes prose poems that walk a wire of anxiety through
contemporary life where -you realize you're naked under your coat, you don't remember a single line, and you'll have to go on like that, you'll have to go on and sing.- And yet the pieces in Centuries are so various and unpredictable and startling, sometimes hyperbolic, often sordid. -The garage smells of turpentine and dirty magazines. commentaries: James George Frazer cites Carpini's history of the Mongols.

book:web_f16729fd.description: A two-volume ethnographic work on the Aboriginal peoples of Victoria, Australia, published in 1878.
commentaries: James George Frazer references this work for information on the Aborigines of Victoria.

commentaries: James George Frazer cites Panzer's book as a source.

book:web_d1cdc815.description: A first-century CE philosophical treatise on the nature of the gods by the Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus.
